Foreshadowing plays a significant role in driving the plot and building suspense in "The Sixth Sense." From the very beginning, subtle hints are dropped to prepare the audience for the revelation that Dr. Crowe is actually a ghost. The opening scene, where Dr. Crowe is shot by a former patient, serves as a pivotal moment. This seemingly random act of violence is later revealed to be the catalyst for the twist ending, where it is discovered that Dr. Crowe has been dead the entire time. The foreshadowing in this scene plants seeds of doubt in the audience's mind and sets the stage for the film's surprising conclusion.

These visual cues serve as foreshadowing elements and contribute to the overall atmosphere of mystery and unease.

In addition to foreshadowing, "The Sixth Sense" utilizes a MacGuffin to drive the plot. The central question of why Cole sees dead people and what his purpose is in helping them becomes the driving force behind the narrative. Both Cole and Dr. Crowe embark on a journey to unravel this mystery together, creating suspense and keeping the audience engaged. The MacGuffin creates a sense of anticipation as the audience eagerly awaits the answers to these questions.

The MacGuffin keeps the audience invested in the story, constantly seeking answers and ultimately rewarded with a thought-provoking and emotionally impactful conclusion.
